title: Rethinking Benign Relearning: Syntax as the Hidden Driver of Unlearning Failures
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Forgotten knowledge resurfaces after fine-tuning on benign data that shares surface structure with it, but not on data that shares only its topic.
layout: 2 stacked phases, top-to-bottom, branching arrows, color-highlighted text spans
description: The figure has two horizontal bands separated by a dashed line. The top band, Phase I Unlearning, shows a building icon and a gray box labeled Data Removal Request. The box holds a sentence with the entity highlighted in purple and the template phrases highlighted in pink. An arrow labeled Unlearning leads from a Base robot to an Unlearned robot carrying an eraser. The bottom band, Phase II Relearning, shows the Unlearned robot on the left with a branching arrow to two gray boxes. The upper box is Fine-tuning on Topically Relevant Data. It repeats the purple entity in a different sentence. Its query Q/A shows a smiling robot giving a wrong answer, so the information is not recovered. The lower box is Fine-tuning on Syntactically Similar Data. It repeats the pink template with different entities. Its query Q/A shows a startled robot with an alarm, and the answer leaks the forgotten name in bold. Color-coded highlights guide the eye.
caption: Overview of unlearning and benign relearning. Phase I (Unlearning): the base model is updated to forget the removal request data. Phase II (Relearning): the unlearned model is fine-tuned on benign data disjoint from the removal request. In the first scenario, fine-tuning is performed on the topically related samples that use the same entities but present them in a different format, and this does not restore forgotten information. In the second scenario, fine-tuning is performed on syntactically similar samples with the same format but different entities, and this enables the model to recover forgotten information when answering target query Q).
abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove specific content from trained models while preserving overall performance. However, the phenomenon of benign relearning, in which forgotten information reemerges even from benign fine-tuning data, reveals that existing unlearning methods remain fundamentally fragile. A common explanation attributes this effect to topical relevance, but we find this account insufficient. Through systematic analysis, we demonstrate that syntactic similarity, rather than topicality, is the primary driver: across benchmarks, syntactically similar data consistently trigger recovery even without topical overlap, due to their alignment in representations and gradients with the forgotten content. Motivated by this insight, we introduce syntactic diversification, which paraphrases the original forget queries into heterogeneous structures prior to unlearning. This approach effectively suppresses benign relearning, accelerates forgetting, and substantially alleviates the trade-off between unlearning efficacy and model utility.
